stimuli.text: The temperature of a liquid, in degrees Celsius, is modeled by a differentiable function $$H$$ of time $$t$$, in minutes. Selected values are shown.
The table gives values of the differentiable functions $$f$$ and $$g$$ and their derivatives.

table.caption: Values of f, f′, g and g′

stimuli.text: Water flows into a tank at a rate of $$R(t)$$ gallons per minute, where $$R$$ is a continuous function of time $$t$$ in minutes. Selected values are shown.
A particle moves along the x-axis. Its velocity is given by $$v(t) = 2\sin\left(\frac{t^2}{2}\right) - 1$$ for $$0 \leq t \leq 4$$. At time $$t = 0$$ the particle is at position $$x = 4$$.

A particle moves in the xy-plane so that for $$0 \leq t \leq 3$$, $$\frac{dx}{dt} = 2\sin\left(\frac{t^2}{3}\right) + 1$$ and $$\frac{dy}{dt} = \cos(t)\,e^{t/4}$$. At $$t = 0$$ the particle is at $$(2, 1)$$.
A particle moves along the x-axis with velocity $$v(t) = 3t^{2} - 18t + 24$$ for $$t \geq 0$$. At time $$t = 0$$ the particle is at $$x = 4$$.
People enter an amusement park at a rate modeled by a differentiable function $$P$$, where $$P(t)$$ is measured in people per minute and $$t$$ is measured in minutes. Selected values are shown.
A function $$f$$ has derivatives of all orders. Selected values are $$f(2) = -4$$, $$f'(2) = -5$$, $$f''(2) = -5$$ and $$f'''(2) = -2$$. For all $$x$$, $$|f^{(4)}(x)| \leq 6$$.

questions.stem: What is the average rate of change of $$H$$ over the interval $$2 \leq t \leq 10$$, in degrees Celsius per minute?

options.why: This is the average temperature, not the average rate of change.
This divides time by temperature, which is upside down.
This is the total change in temperature; it still needs to be divided by the elapsed time.

questions.explanation: Average rate of change $$= \frac{H(10) - H(2)}{10 - 2} = \frac{17 - 54}{8} = -\frac{37}{8}$$ degrees per minute.

questions.stem: Let $$y = f(x)$$ be the solution to $$\frac{dy}{dx} = x + y$$ with $$f(0) = 3$$. Using the tangent line at $$x = 0$$, what is the approximation of $$f(0.1)$$?

options.why: Sign error in the step.
This adds the slope without multiplying by the step 0.1.
This is only the estimated change; add it to f(a).

questions.explanation: At $$(0, 3)$$, $$\frac{dy}{dx} = 3$$. The tangent line gives $$f(0.1) \approx 3 + 3(0.1) = 3.3$$.

questions.stem: Which of the following functions is a solution to the differential equation $$y'' + 4y = 0$$?

options.why: $$y'' = 4$$, which does not cancel $$4y$$.

questions.explanation: Substitute each candidate. For $$y = \sin(2x)$$: $$y' = 2\cos(2x)$$, $$y'' = -4\sin(2x) = -4y$$.

questions.stem: If $$\int_0^{3} f(x)\,dx = -6$$ and $$\int_0^{7} f(x)\,dx = 11$$, what is $$\int_{3}^{7} \left(2f(x) + 4\right)dx$$?

options.why: This forgets to multiply the integral of $$f$$ by $$2$$.
The integral of the constant $$4$$ over an interval of length $$4$$ is $$16$$, not $$4$$.
This adds the two given integrals; the integral from a to b is their difference.

questions.explanation: $$\int_{3}^{7} f(x)\,dx = \int_0^{7} f - \int_0^{3} f = 17$$. By linearity, the requested integral is $$2 \cdot 17 + 4 \cdot 4 = 50$$.

questions.stem: What is $$\lim_{x \to -4} \frac{x^{2} + 5x + 4}{x + 4}$$?

options.why: The expression is undefined at the point, but its outputs nearby approach a single number, so the limit exists.
Substituting gives $$\frac{0}{0}$$, an indeterminate form, not the value 0.
Correct. The numerator factors as $$(x + 4)(x + 1)$$. Cancel $$x + 4$$ and substitute: $$-4 - (-1) = -3$$.
This adds the roots. After cancelling, the expression is $$x + 1$$, which approaches $$-3$$.

questions.explanation: Direct substitution gives $$\frac{0}{0}$$, so factor: $$x^{2} + 5x + 4 = (x + 4)(x + 1)$$. For $$x \neq -4$$ the expression equals $$x + 1$$, so the limit is $$-4 - (-1) = -3$$.

options.why: The derivative of $$e^x$$ is $$e^x$$, which equals $$e$$ at 1, not 1.
The derivative of $$-2x^2$$ is $$-4x$$.
This uses $$\ln 1 = 0$$, but the derivative of $$\ln x$$ is $$\frac{1}{x}$$, which is 1 at $$x = 1$$.

questions.explanation: Differentiate term by term: $$f'(x) = 3e^{x} + \frac{-3}{x} - 4x$$. At $$x = 1$$ this is $$3e - 7$$.

questions.stem: Using the line tangent to $$f(x) = \sqrt{x}$$ at $$x = 16$$, what is the approximation of $$\sqrt{13}$$?

options.why: Sign error: the change in x is added, not subtracted.
The derivative of $$\sqrt{x}$$ is $$\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}$$; this forgets the 2.
This uses slope $$\frac{1}{2}$$ instead of $$f'(16) = \frac{1}{8}$$.

questions.stem: What is $$\int_0^{\infty} e^{-2x}\,dx$$?

options.why: The exponential decays fast enough for the area to be finite.
The antiderivative of $$e^{-kx}$$ has a factor $$\frac{1}{k}$$, not $$k$$.
Sign error: the integrand is positive, so the integral is positive.
Correct. $$\lim_{b \to \infty}\left[-\frac{1}{2}e^{-2x}\right]_0^b = \frac{1}{2}$$.

questions.explanation: $$\int_0^b e^{-2x}dx = \frac{1}{2}\left(1 - e^{-2b}\right) \to \frac{1}{2}$$.

questions.stem: What is the absolute maximum value of $$f(x) = x^{3} - 27x + 5$$ on the closed interval $$[-5, 5]$$?

options.why: Correct. Compare $$f$$ at the critical points $$x = \pm 3$$ and the endpoints: the largest value is $$59$$.
This is the absolute minimum value.
This is a candidate value, but not the largest one. Check every critical point and both endpoints.
This is a candidate value, but not the largest one. Check every critical point and both endpoints.

questions.stem: For the curve $$x^2 + xy + y^2 = 13$$, what is $$\frac{dy}{dx}$$ at the point $$(-3, -1)$$?

options.why: Sign error when solving for dy/dx.
Correct. $$2x + y + x\frac{dy}{dx} + 2y\frac{dy}{dx} = 0$$, so $$\frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{2x + y}{x + 2y}$$.
This differentiates $$xy$$ as $$y$$, forgetting the product rule term $$x\frac{dy}{dx}$$.
This ignores the $$xy$$ term entirely.

questions.explanation: Implicit differentiation with the product rule on $$xy$$: $$2x + (y + xy') + 2yy' = 0$$. Solving, $$y' = -\frac{2x + y}{x + 2y}$$; at $$(-3, -1)$$, $$y' = -\frac{7}{5}$$.

questions.stem: Which of the following gives the length of the curve $$y = \sin x$$ from $$x = 0$$ to $$x = 3$$?

options.why: Correct. Arc length integrates $$\sqrt{1 + [f'(x)]^2}$$.
The derivative must be squared.
The integrand needs a square root and a squared derivative.
This squares the function instead of its derivative.

questions.explanation: For $$y = f(x)$$, $$L = \int_a^b \sqrt{1 + [f'(x)]^2}\,dx$$, and here $$f'(x) = \cos x$$.

questions.stem: What is the area of one petal of the rose $$r = 2\sin(3\theta)$$?

options.why: The radius must be squared.
The integral of $$\sin^2$$ produces a factor of $$\pi$$.
This leaves out the factor $$\frac{1}{2}$$ in the polar area formula.
Correct. $$\frac{1}{2}\int_0^{\pi/3} 4\sin^2(3\theta)\,d\theta = \frac{4\pi}{12}$$.

questions.explanation: One petal runs from $$\theta = 0$$ to $$\theta = \frac{\pi}{3}$$, where $$r = 0$$. Using $$\sin^2 u = \frac{1 - \cos 2u}{2}$$, the area is $$\frac{4}{2}\cdot\frac{\pi}{2\cdot 3} = \frac{\pi}{3}$$.

questions.stem: What is the sum of $$\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} 3\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)^n$$?

options.why: Correct. Geometric with first term $$3$$ and ratio $$-\frac{1}{2}$$.
The first term depends on the starting index; check the term for the first value of n.
This divides by $$r$$ instead of $$1 - r$$.
The formula is $$\frac{a}{1 - r}$$, not $$\frac{a}{1 + r}$$.

questions.explanation: $$|r| = \left|-\frac{1}{2}\right| < 1$$, so the series converges to $$\frac{3}{1 - \left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)} = 2$$.

questions.stem: Let $$h(x) = f(x)g(x)$$. What is $$h'(4)$$?

options.why: The derivative of a product is not the product of the derivatives.
The product rule adds the two terms; subtraction belongs to the quotient rule.

questions.stem: What is the area of the region enclosed by the curves $$x = y^2$$ and $$x = 3y$$?

options.why: An area is never negative; this subtracts the curves in the wrong order.
This is the area under the parabola alone.
Correct. $$\int_0^{3} (3y - y^2)\,dy$$: right curve minus left curve.
This is the area under the line alone.

questions.explanation: The curves meet at $$0$$ and $$3$$. Area $$= \int_0^{3} (3u - u^2)\,du = \frac{3u^2}{2} - \frac{u^3}{3}\Big|_0^{3} = \frac{9}{2}$$.

questions.stem: Let $$P_{3}(x)$$ be the degree-3 Taylor polynomial for $$f$$ about $$x = 2$$, and suppose $$|f^{(4)}(x)| \leq 12$$ for all $$x$$. What is the Lagrange error bound for $$|f(\frac{21}{10}) - P_{3}(\frac{21}{10})|$$?

options.why: Correct. $$\frac{12}{4!}\left(\frac{1}{10}\right)^{4}$$.
The distance from the center must be raised to the power n + 1.
This uses the degree n instead of n + 1 for the factorial and power.
This forgets to divide by $$(n + 1)!$$.

questions.stem: The sum of $$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n^{2}}$$ is approximated by its first 8 terms. What is the smallest upper bound on the error given by the alternating series error bound?

options.why: This skips a term: the bound is the very next term.
Correct. The error is at most the first omitted term.
This is the last term used, not the first one omitted.
The exponent stays the same as in the series.

questions.explanation: The terms alternate, decrease in size and approach 0, so $$|S - S_{8}| \leq b_{9} = \frac{1}{9^{2}}$$.

questions.stem: The derivative of a function $$f$$ is $$f'(x) = (x + 2)^2(x - 2)$$. On which intervals is $$f$$ increasing?

options.why: Correct. The squared factor is never negative, so the sign of $$f'$$ matches $$x - 2$$.
Here f′ < 0 because $$x - 2 < 0$$.
On $$-2 < x < 2$$ the factor $$x - 2$$ is negative.
The squared factor does not change sign at $$x = -2$$, so f′ < 0 for $$x < -2$$.

questions.explanation: $$(x + 2)^2 \geq 0$$ for all $$x$$, so $$f'(x) > 0$$ exactly when $$x > 2$$. Note $$f'$$ does not change sign at $$-2$$, so there is no extremum there.

questions.stem: Consider the curve $$x^2 - xy + y^2 = 27$$, for which $$\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{y - 2x}{2y - x}$$. At which points on the curve is the tangent line horizontal?

options.why: These points do not lie on the curve.
These are the y-intercepts; there the slope is 1/2, not 0.
Correct. Horizontal tangents need $$y - 2x = 0$$. Substituting $$y = 2x$$ gives $$3x^2 = 27$$.
These have 2y − x = 0, where the denominator is zero: the tangent lines are vertical.

questions.stem: A function $$f$$ has $$f(-1) = 5$$, $$f'(-1) = 5$$, $$f''(-1) = -4$$ and $$f'''(-1) = 8$$. What is the coefficient of $$(x + 1)^3$$ in the Taylor polynomial for $$f$$ about $$x = -1$$?

options.why: This divides by 3 instead of $$3! = 6$$.
This forgets to divide by $$3!$$.
This is the coefficient of the squared term.

questions.explanation: The coefficient of $$(x + 1)^k$$ is $$\frac{f^{(k)}(-1)}{k!}$$; for $$k = 3$$ it is $$\frac{8}{6} = \frac{4}{3}$$.

questions.stem: What is $$\int_0^{\pi/2} x\cos x\,dx$$?

options.why: Sign error in the integration-by-parts formula.
This evaluates only part of the antiderivative or only one limit.
Correct. Integration by parts, then evaluate at both limits.
This drops the second term produced by integration by parts.

questions.explanation: Use integration by parts: $$\left[x\sin x + \cos x\right]_0^{\pi/2} = \frac{\pi}{2} - 1$$.

questions.stem:
Which of the following series converge?

I. $$\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^n$$

II. $$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n^2}$$

III. $$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^n}{n}$$

options.why: Correct. I: converges (geometric with |r| = 2/3 < 1). II: converges (p-series with p = 2 > 1). III: converges (alternating series test, but the harmonic series diverges).
Check each series with an appropriate test: I converges, II converges, III converges.
Check each series with an appropriate test: I converges, II converges, III converges.
Check each series with an appropriate test: I converges, II converges, III converges.

questions.explanation: Series I converges: geometric with |r| = 2/3 < 1. Series II converges: p-series with p = 2 > 1. Series III converges: alternating series test, but the harmonic series diverges.

options.why: This evaluates the integrand at both limits; the derivative of an accumulation function only uses the variable limit.
This leaves out the derivative of the upper limit, $$3x^{2}$$.
Correct. By the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus with the chain rule, substitute the upper limit and multiply by its derivative.
The integrand must be evaluated at the upper limit, not at x.

questions.stem: Using a trapezoidal sum with the four subintervals indicated by the table, what is the approximation of $$\int_0^{10} R(t)\,dt$$?

options.why: This treats every subinterval as width 2, but the subintervals have unequal widths.
Correct. Multiply each subinterval's width by the appropriate height and add.
This is the left Riemann sum.
This is the right Riemann sum.

questions.explanation: The widths are 2, 1, 4, 3. Average the endpoint heights on each subinterval, multiply by the width and add: $$\frac{121}{2}$$ gallons.

questions.stem: What is $$\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\ln(1 + 3x)}{5x}$$?

options.why: $$\frac{0}{0}$$ is indeterminate; it does not mean the limit is 0.
Correct. The limit has the form $$\frac{0}{0}$$, so L'Hospital's Rule applies: $$\frac{3/(1 + 3x)}{5}$$.
This leaves out the chain-rule factor when differentiating the numerator.
This differentiates the numerator and denominator but then inverts the ratio, or applies the rule incorrectly.

questions.explanation: Direct substitution gives $$\frac{0}{0}$$. Differentiate the numerator and denominator separately (L'Hospital's Rule): $$\frac{3/(1 + 3x)}{5}$$, which gives $$\frac{3}{5}$$.

questions.stem: What is the interval of convergence of $$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{(x - 3)^n}{n\cdot 3^n}$$?

options.why: The radius is 3, from the factor $$3^n$$.
Correct. Ratio test gives $$|x - 3| < 3$$; the left endpoint gives an alternating harmonic series (converges), the right endpoint the harmonic series (diverges).
The left endpoint gives $$\sum \frac{(-1)^n}{n}$$, which converges.
The endpoints are reversed: the right endpoint gives the divergent harmonic series.

questions.explanation: Ratio: $$\left|\frac{(x - 3)^{n+1}}{(n + 1)3^{n+1}}\cdot\frac{n\,3^n}{(x - 3)^n}\right| \to \frac{|x - 3|}{3}$$, so $$|x - 3| < 3$$. At $$x = 6$$: $$\sum \frac{1}{n}$$ diverges. At $$x = 0$$: $$\sum \frac{(-1)^n}{n}$$ converges.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes $$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^n}{\sqrt{n}}$$?

options.text: It converges, but to a negative sum only if the first term is negative.
options.why: This statement is not a classification of convergence.
Not this one: alternating series test, but p = 1/2 for the absolute values.
Correct. alternating series test, but p = 1/2 for the absolute values.
Not this one: alternating series test, but p = 1/2 for the absolute values.

questions.explanation: Test the absolute values first, then the series itself: alternating series test, but p = 1/2 for the absolute values.

questions.stem: What is $$\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sqrt{x + 36} - 6}{x}$$?

options.why: This forgets that the conjugate denominator is $$\sqrt{x + 36} + 6$$, which approaches $$12$$, not $$6$$.
Correct. Rationalizing gives $$\frac{1}{\sqrt{x + 36} + 6}$$, which approaches $$\frac{1}{12}$$.
Substitution gives $$\frac{0}{0}$$, an indeterminate form.
The expression is undefined at 0, but rationalizing shows the outputs approach a single number.

questions.explanation: Multiply by $$\frac{\sqrt{x + 36} + 6}{\sqrt{x + 36} + 6}$$. The numerator becomes $$x$$, which cancels, leaving $$\frac{1}{\sqrt{x + 36} + 6} \to \frac{1}{12}$$.

questions.stem: For the curve $$x = t^2$$, $$y = t^{3} + 3t$$, what is $$\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}$$ at $$t = 2$$?

options.why: This divides $$y''(t)$$ by $$x''(t)$$, which is not the second derivative.
This is $$\frac{dy}{dx}$$, the first derivative.
This forgets to divide by $$\frac{dx}{dt}$$.
Correct. Differentiate $$\frac{dy}{dx}$$ with respect to $$t$$, then divide by $$\frac{dx}{dt} = 2t$$.

questions.explanation: $$\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{3t^2 + 3}{2t} = \frac{3t}{2} + \frac{3}{2t}$$. Its $$t$$-derivative is $$\frac{3}{2} - \frac{3}{2t^2}$$, which is $$\frac{9}{8}$$ at $$t = 2$$. Dividing by $$2t = 4$$ gives $$\frac{9}{32}$$.

questions.stem: What is the slope of the line tangent to the polar curve $$r = 3 + 2\cos\theta$$ at $$\theta = \frac{\pi}{2}$$?

options.why: Correct. $$\frac{dy}{d\theta} = -2$$ and $$\frac{dx}{d\theta} = -3$$.
Sign error in $$\frac{dx}{d\theta} = r'\cos\theta - r\sin\theta$$.
This is $$\frac{dx/d\theta}{dy/d\theta}$$, upside down.
This is $$\frac{dr}{d\theta}$$, which is not the slope.

questions.explanation: With $$x = r\cos\theta$$ and $$y = r\sin\theta$$: at $$\theta = \frac{\pi}{2}$$, $$r = 3$$ and $$r' = (-2)$$. So $$\frac{dy}{d\theta} = r'\sin\theta + r\cos\theta = -2$$ and $$\frac{dx}{d\theta} = r'\cos\theta - r\sin\theta = -3$$; the slope is $$\frac{2}{3}$$.

questions.stem: What is the value of $$\int_{0}^{1} \sqrt{1 + x^3}\,dx$$?

options.why: This is a single rectangle using the right endpoint, a rough estimate rather than the integral.
This integrates over only half of the interval.
This is the change in the integrand, not the integral.
Correct. Use the calculator's numerical integration.

questions.explanation: On a graphing calculator, $$\int_{0}^{1} \sqrt{1 + x^3}\,dx \approx 1.111$$.

questions.stem: A population satisfies $$\frac{dP}{dt} = 0.002P(500 - P)$$ with $$P(0) = 225$$. What is $$\lim_{t \to \infty} P(t)$$?

options.why: This is where the population grows fastest, not its limit.
Logistic growth levels off; it does not grow without bound.
The population changes from its initial value; it is not constant.
Correct. The carrying capacity: the factor $$(500 - P)$$ makes growth stop at $$P = 500$$.

questions.explanation: Since $$0 < P(0) < 500$$, $$\frac{dP}{dt} > 0$$ and $$P$$ increases toward the equilibrium $$P = 500$$.

questions.stem: The temperature of a room, in degrees Fahrenheit, is modeled by $$H(t) = 46 + 9\sin\left(\frac{t}{4}\right)e^{-t/20}$$, where $$t$$ is measured in hours. What is the instantaneous rate of change of the temperature at $$t = 14$$, in degrees Fahrenheit per hour?

options.why: This multiplies the rate by the time, which is not a rate.
This is the temperature itself, not its rate of change.
This is the average rate of change over $$0 \leq t \leq 14$$, not the instantaneous rate.
Correct. The calculator's numerical derivative of $$H$$ at $$t = 14$$ gives -0.968; the temperature is decreasing.

questions.explanation: The instantaneous rate of change is $$H'(14) \approx -0.968$$ degrees Fahrenheit per hour, from the calculator's numerical derivative.

questions.stem: A function $$f$$ has $$f(-1) = 1$$, $$f'(-1) = -3$$ and $$f''(-1) = 2$$. Using the second-degree Taylor polynomial for $$f$$ about $$x = -1$$, what is the approximation of $$f(-1.1)$$?

options.why: This is the tangent-line (first-degree) approximation.
The quadratic term must use $$(x - a)^2$$, not $$(x - a)$$.
This forgets to divide the second derivative by $$2!$$.

questions.stem: What is the area of the region enclosed by the graphs of $$y = 2\cos\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)$$ and $$y = x^2 - 1$$?

options.why: This is the area under the top curve only.
This adds the absolute values of the curves instead of subtracting.
Correct. The curves meet at $$x \approx -1.557$$ and $$x \approx 1.557$$; integrate top minus bottom.
This is the distance between the intersection points, not an area.

questions.explanation: Store the intersection x-values from the calculator, then $$\int_{-1.557}^{1.557} \left(2\cos\frac{x}{2} - (x^2 - 1)\right)dx \approx 6.215$$.

questions.stem: A particle moves in the plane with $$x'(t) = \cos\left(\frac{t^2}{2}\right)$$ and $$y'(t) = e^{t/2}$$. What is the total distance the particle travels from $$t = 0$$ to $$t = 2$$?

options.why: Correct. Integrate the speed $$\sqrt{x'(t)^2 + y'(t)^2}$$.
This is the speed at the final time.
This is the straight-line distance between the start and end points.
This adds the component displacements instead of integrating the speed.
Sign error in the linear factors.
The numerator is not a multiple of the derivative of the denominator, so this is not a single logarithm.
The coefficients are matched to the wrong factors.

questions.explanation: Factor the denominator as $$(x - 4)(x - 2)$$. Solve $$-x = A(x - 2) + B(x - 4)$$: substituting $$x = 4$$ and $$x = 2$$ gives $$A = -2$$ and $$B = 1$$. Each piece integrates to a logarithm.

questions.stem: Let $$f(x) = \sqrt{x}\,\cos x$$. What is the value of $$f'(2.5)$$?

options.why: This is the function value, not the derivative.
Correct. Use the calculator's numerical derivative (or the correct rule) at the given input.
This is the derivative at $$x = 3.5$$, not at $$x = 2.5$$.
This multiplies the derivatives of the factors instead of using the product rule.

questions.explanation: On a graphing calculator, evaluate $$\left.\frac{d}{dx}\left(\sqrt{x}\,\cos x\right)\right|_{x = 2.5} \approx -1.200$$.

questions.stem: What is the coefficient of $$x^{3}$$ in the Maclaurin series for $$f(x) = \sin(2x)$$?

options.why: Sign error: check the sign pattern of the series.
The denominator is $$n!$$, not $$n$$.
The constant must be raised to the same power as x.
Correct. Substitute into the known Maclaurin series.

questions.explanation: Replace $$x$$ by $$2x$$ in the series for $$\sin x$$: the $$x^{3}$$ term is $$\frac{-(2x)^{3}}{3!}$$, so the coefficient is $$-\frac{4}{3}$$.

questions.stem: Sand is added to a pile at a rate modeled by $$R(t) = 26 + 4\sin\left(\frac{t}{5}\right)\sqrt{t + 1}$$ cubic feet per hour, for $$0 \leq t \leq 11$$. At time $$t = 0$$ the pile contains 294 cubic feet of sand. How much sand is in the pile at $$t = 11$$?

options.why: This assumes the rate stays at R(T) for the whole time.
This is only the sand added; include the initial amount.
This adds the rate at one instant, not the accumulated amount.

questions.explanation: Amount = initial amount + accumulated change = $$294 + \int_0^{11} R(t)\,dt \approx 294 + 372.155 = 666.155$$ cubic feet.

questions.stem: What is the absolute maximum value of $$f(x) = x^2e^{-x/3} + \frac{\sin x}{4}$$ on the interval $$[0, 10]$$?

options.why: Correct. Graph f on the calculator and find its maximum on the interval, checking the endpoints too.
This evaluates f at the critical point of the first term alone; the sine term shifts the maximum.
This is where the maximum occurs (the x-value), not the maximum value.
This is the value at the right endpoint, which is not the largest.

questions.explanation: On the calculator, the maximum of $$f$$ on $$[0, 10]$$ occurs at $$x \approx 6.889$$, where $$f(x) \approx 4.918$$. The endpoint values are smaller.

questions.stem: What is the area of the region bounded by the polar curve $$r = 4 + 0.5\sin^2\theta + \frac{\cos 3\theta}{2}$$ and the rays $$\theta = 0$$ and $$\theta = \frac{\pi}{2}$$?

options.why: Correct. $$\frac{1}{2}\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}} r^2\,d\theta$$ on the calculator.
This leaves out the factor $$\frac{1}{2}$$.
The radius must be squared.
This divides by $$\pi$$, which is not part of the formula.

questions.explanation: $$A = \frac{1}{2}\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \left(4 + 0.5\sin^2\theta + \frac{\cos 3\theta}{2}\right)^2 d\theta \approx 13.526$$.

questions.stem: A function $$f$$ has $$f(2) = -2$$, $$f'(2) = 2$$, $$f''(2) = -6$$ and $$f'''(2) = -4$$. What is the coefficient of $$(x - 2)^3$$ in the Taylor polynomial for $$f$$ about $$x = 2$$?

options.why: This divides by 3 instead of $$3! = 6$$.
This forgets to divide by $$3!$$.
This is the coefficient of the squared term.

questions.explanation: The coefficient of $$(x - 2)^k$$ is $$\frac{f^{(k)}(2)}{k!}$$; for $$k = 3$$ it is $$\frac{-4}{6} = -\frac{2}{3}$$.

questions.stem: What is the coefficient of $$x^{4}$$ in the Maclaurin series for $$f(x) = \frac{1}{1 - 3x}$$?

options.why: The coefficient is the ratio raised to the nth power.
Correct. Substitute into the known Maclaurin series.
The geometric series has no factorials.
Sign error: check the sign pattern of the series.

questions.explanation: $$\frac{1}{1 - u} = \sum u^n$$ with $$u = 3x$$: the coefficient of $$x^{4}$$ is $$3^{4} = 81$$.

questions.stem: Let $$R$$ be the region bounded by $$y = \sqrt{x}\,e^{-x/4} + 0.2$$, the x-axis, $$x = 0$$, and $$x = 5$$. What is the volume of the solid generated when $$R$$ is revolved about the line $$y = -1$$?

options.why: This revolves about the x-axis.
Correct. Washers with outer radius $$f(x) + 1$$ and inner radius $$1$$.
This leaves out the factor of π.
